Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures

Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then- Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on ToolBench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross- category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single- tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (_k_=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt- oss-120b). We characterize a stub-hallucination failure mode (the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names) that acts as a double-edged sword: on simple queries PtR’s stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, yet on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs. We further analyze token overhead and show that PtR’s extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction — one that can be driven by a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtP’s top-1 retrieval score).

### 1 Introduction

Tool-augmented LLM agents operate over registries of thousands of APIs under tight context constraints (Qin et al., 2024b; Patil et al., 2024). The dominant approach directly embeds the user query and retrieves the top-_k_ most similar APIs before passing them to the planner (Patil et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024b; Yuan et al., 2024), assuming the semantic gap between user intent and API documentation is small enough to bridge by embedding alone. Recent work shows this assumption often fails (Shi et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024), motivating an alternative direction where the LLM generates query reformulations or plans before retrieval to better express functional intent (Fang and Glass, 2026). However, such works propose training-dependent systems aimed at improving retrieval quality, rather than characterizing when and why each approach is preferable. The underlying paradigm comparison remains unexplored.

Prior work has studied retrieval-side improvements: Tool Retrieval Bridge (Chen et al., 2026) rewrites queries into retriever-friendly forms; Re-Invoke (Chen et al., 2024) enriches tool descriptions with synthetic queries; TaskBench (Shen et al., 2024) benchmarks the decompose-then-select pipeline; and Tool-MVR (Ma et al., 2025) treats stub hallucination as a bug to fix (we show it is a feature on complex queries). ToolFlood (Jawad and Brunel, 2026) and a recent survey (Qin et al., 2024a) provide broader context on retrieval robustness and tool learning. A related line of work uses LLM-guided tool selection, where the model draws on parametric knowledge rather than vector retrieval: HuggingGPT (Shen et al., 2023) has ChatGPT select specialized models from HuggingFace; AnyTool (Du et al., 2024) uses GPT-4 to hierarchically narrow API categories;

The closest prior work to the paradigm we study is TOOLQP (Fang and Glass, 2026), which generates multi- round query reformulations to improve API retrieval, trained with reinforcement learning. Our approach differs in three ways: stubs are generated in a single zero-shot prompt call with no training, we generate hypothetical function signatures rather than query reformulations, and we study PtR as a controlled paradigm rather than proposing a new system. Despite this active area, no prior work has directly compared these two retrieval paradigms in a controlled setting at large registry scale, characterized how the trade-off changes with query complexity, or analyzed how retrieval differences cascade into planner behavior.

We term the dominant paradigm Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP) and the alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR), and present the first systematic apples-to-apples comparison at industrial scale (50k APIs). A key analytical lens we introduce is Intent-Registry Coupling: the semantic gap between how users describe tasks and how APIs are documented. Our PtR instantiation generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures) as retrieval queries in a single zero-shot prompt call with no training. Our contributions: **(1)** a complexity- dependent crossover (RtP wins on simple queries, PtR wins on multi-tool queries) robust to retrieval budget, registry size, and model family; **(2)** a characterization of stub hallucination as a dual mechanism: it degrades retrieval when queries have high Intent-Registry Coupling, and improves it when they do not; **(3)** an analysis of token overhead showing that directing single-tool queries to RtP and multi-tool queries to PtR reduces discovery-call overhead by ∼36% with no retrieval quality loss, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction consistent with prior work on complexity-aware retrieval (Jeong et al., 2024).

discovery model (temperature=0, retrieval budget _k_=5). Let T be the tool registry, _q_ the user query, _d<sub>t</sub>_ the documentation of tool _t_, \(\mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)\) the cosine similarity between embeddings, and \(\pi(\cdot)\) the agent’s execution plan given a retrieved tool set.

**RtP** embeds the raw query and retrieves the top-_k_ most similar APIs: \(R_{\mathrm{RtP}}(q)=\mathrm{TopK}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathrm{sim}(q,d_t)\); the planner then produces plan \(\pi_{\mathrm{RtP}}(q,R_{\mathrm{RtP}}(q))\).

**PtR** first sends _q_ to the planner _without_ any tool definitions, generating stubs _S(q_)={_s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>m</sub>_} (JSON objects with a hypothesized tool name and reasoning). Each stub is embedded and matched against the index; the union of top-_k_ results (deduplicated, re-ranked) forms \(R_{\mathrm{PtR}}(q)=\mathrm{TopK}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathrm{max}_{s\in S(q)}\mathrm{sim}(s,d_t)\), which is passed back to the planner to produce \(\pi_{\mathrm{PtR}}(q,R_{\mathrm{PtR}}(q))\).

An unfiltered baseline is infeasible at this scale: ToolBench categories contain up to 4,455 APIs (Sports) and 3,583 (Data), and Ground-Truth APIs are distributed across each category such that any fixed-size truncation misses them in the vast majority of cases.

## 2.2 Data and Metrics

ToolBench (Qin et al., 2024b) provides three test subsets: **G1** (single-tool, _n_=200), **G2** (intra-category multi- tool, _n_=200), and **G3** (cross-category multi-tool, _n_=100; smaller set, so G3 differences have lower statistical power). We report retrieval **recall** and **precision** computed at the fixed budget _k_=5 against the Ground- Truth API set from each query’s ToolBench gold trajectory (all APIs executed in the reference solution). RtP retrieval is deterministic (the query is embedded by GTE-base, a fixed model, and matched against the FAISS index via exact nearest-neighbor search; no LLM call, no sampling), so its precision and recall carry no run-to-run variance and are reported without a standard deviation. All remaining quantities -- PtR’s precision and recall, and pass rate for both architectures -- are averaged over 4 independent runs and reported as mean \(\pm\)std, since both stub generation and planner output vary across runs. Statistical comparisons use a one-sample _t_-test for precision and recall (PtR’s 4-run mean vs. the deterministic RtP value) and a two-sample _t_-test for pass rate. All experiments use the full 46,984-API registry unless otherwise noted.

_Evaluation proxy._ We evaluate against ToolBench gold trajectories as a retrieval proxy rather than end-to-end API execution. Trajectory fidelity (at least 96%; §4.3) supports this as a valid proxy for planner behavior: the planner almost always selects from the retrieved set, so retrieval quality upper-bounds task completion. Parameter correctness and final answer quality are not assessed and constitute a limitation noted in §5.

## 3 Results

### 3.1 Main Results

Figure 2 presents the central finding (full numerical results in Appendix A). RtP leads all G1 metrics: recall 0.372 vs. 0.289\(\pm\)0.010 (_p_=0.002), precision 0.274 vs. 0.209\(\pm\)0.008 (_p\<_0.001), pass rate 0.884\(\pm\)0.015 vs. 0.840\(\pm\)0.024 (_p_=0.022). The pattern reverses on multi-tool queries: PtR leads G2 recall 0.188\(\pm\)0.007 vs. 0.143 (_p\<_0.001), precision 0.204\(\pm\)0.007 vs. 0.167 (_p_=0.039), and pass rate 0.855\(\pm\)0.020 vs. 0.747\(\pm\)0.015 (_p\<_0.001). On G3 (_n_=100), PtR maintains a directional advantage: recall 0.172\(\pm\)0.008 vs. 0.160 and pass rate 0.820\(\pm\)0.014 vs. 0.732\(\pm\)0.010 (_p\<_0.001); the recall difference does not reach significance, reflecting the smaller G3 sample. Panel (b) shows the per-query breakdown: on G1, RtP wins on 63 queries vs. PtR’s 33; on G2 the pattern flips, with PtR winning on 69 queries vs. RtP’s 30.

1 shows the crossover holds at every retrieval budget from _k_=1 to _k_=20. PtR’s G2 advantage grows with _k_ (from +0.014 at _k_=1 to +0.066 at _k_=20) because each stub contributes its own top-_k_ candidates, providing broader multi-faceted coverage as _k_ increases. RtP’s G1 advantage is stable across _k_.

### 3.2 Scaling Behavior

Figure 3 shows recall for both G1 and G2, alongside **tool selection divergence** (fraction of queries where the two architectures retrieve entirely non-overlapping top-_k_ API sets) across sub-registries from 1k to 47k APIs (5 random seeds, proportional category sampling). Both recall curves degrade with registry size but the RtP–PtR gap is stable across scales (recall std _\<_ 0.012): RtP maintains its G1 advantage and PtR maintains its G2 advantage at every registry size tested. Tool selection divergence increases from 88% at 1k to 98% at 47k ( 10), confirming the architecture choice is a structural property that becomes more consequential at scale. Per-subset divergence values for the full registry are reported in Appendix D.

### 3.3 Agent Trajectory Divergence

We define the _agent trajectory_ as the set of APIs the planner names and the steps it describes in its output. Since we do not execute API calls, all measurements reflect the planner’s _intended_ behavior. Trajectory divergence measures whether the two architectures lead to the same intended tool calls (via Jaccard similarity). Trajectory fidelity measures whether the planner stays within the retrieved set (100% = planner always names an API it was given).

Trajectory fidelity is at least 96% across all subsets: the planner almost always selects from the retrieved set, confirming retrieval is the binding constraint on what the agent can do. Figure 4 shows five dimensions of trajectory divergence. The Jaccard similarity of planner-selected APIs decreases from 0.40 (G1) to 0.28 (G3), meaning even at the planner-selection level the architectures produce increasingly different tool call sequences. PtR’s planner uses a higher fraction of retrieved APIs (27-29% vs. 21-27%), suggesting its stub- guided retrieval produces a more coherent candidate set that the planner trusts. On G3, PtR generates more ambitious plans (4.1 intended steps, 1.4 APIs named) while RtP produces sparser plans (3.6 steps, 1.1 APIs named), suggesting PtR’s multi-stub retrieval gives the planner richer material to work with. ## 4 Discussion

### 4.1 Why the Crossover Occurs

The crossover reflects the two faces of Intent-Registry Coupling. On G1, coupling is high: the raw query often contains the API’s name or brand directly, giving RtP a direct embedding match while a planning step only abstracts away this signal. On G2/G3, coupling is low: a single embedding cannot capture multifaceted intent. G2 queries require a mean of 6.5 Ground-Truth APIs vs. 5.2 on G1; PtR generates 2.4-2.5 stubs per query, each anchoring to a different functional sub-need and retrieving independently. PtR’s G2 advantage grows with _k_ (from +0.014 at _k_=1 to +0.066 at _k_=20) because each stub contributes its own top-_k_ candidates.

A natural concern is whether PtR’s G2 advantage is simply an artifact of broader search: with _m_≈2.4 stubs each retrieving top-_k_, PtR explores ∼2.4_k_ candidates before returning _k_ to the planner, while RtP searches exactly _k_. The _k_-ablation ( 1) directly addresses this: at budget-equivalent _k_=10 (matching PtR’s effective search width at _k_=5), RtP G2 recall reaches 0.186, nearly identical to PtR at _k_=5 (0.184 in the ablation; 0.188\(\pm\)0.007 in the main experiment). However, this budget-equivalent RtP passes _k_=10 APIs to the planner, halving precision relative to PtR’s _k_=5 output. The G1 finding is unaffected: even at _k_=10, RtP G1 recall (0.453) far exceeds PtR at _k_=5 (0.279). Together, these results confirm that the crossover reflects structural properties of query-registry coupling rather than search breadth alone.

### 4.2 Stub Hallucination: The Mechanism

PtR generates 79-99% unique stub names across subsets ( 4), confirming the LLM is hallucinating tool names from scratch rather than recalling real API names. The cosine similarity between correct and incorrect stub-API matches is virtually identical (e.g., G1: 0.874 vs. 0.872; similarly small gaps on G2 and G3), meaning the embedding space provides _no signal_ to distinguish good routing from bad. Only 40.6% of G1 stubs and 24.8% of G3 stubs match a relevant API at all. Despite this, G3 recall favors PtR because multi-stub _coverage_ compensates for individual stub mismatches: 2.5 stubs per query span different functional domains, and finding the right tool for each sub-need does not require every stub to succeed.  2 shows representative examples of each mode.

## 4.3 Discovery as the Binding Constraint

Trajectory fidelity (at least 96%, Figure 4e) confirms the planner almost always selects from the retrieved set, making retrieval the bottleneck. As a result, architecture choice at retrieval time fully determines downstream behavior: PtR’s planner generates more ambitious plans on G3 (4.1 intended steps, 1.4 APIs named vs. 3.6 steps, 1.1 APIs) and uses a higher fraction of retrieved APIs (27-29% vs. 21-27%), reflecting the broader, more coherent candidate sets produced by stub-guided retrieval.

PtR’s discovery call adds ∼75-104% token overhead (Appendix E,  8); on G1 this hurts (-0.072 recall) while on G2 it pays off (+0.042 recall). Beyond token cost, this discovery call sits on the critical path: because discovery and retrieval are sequential, PtR adds one full LLM round-trip of latency before retrieval and planning begin, so the overhead is both a token cost and a wall-clock latency penalty. Complexity- adaptive routing (using RtP for G1, PtR for G2/G3) saves ∼16% of total inference tokens, or ∼36% of the PtR discovery-call overhead, with no retrieval quality loss relative to always selecting the better architecture per subset, and eliminates the extra round-trip entirely for G1-type queries. The crossover maps naturally onto single-tool vs. multi-tool intent; practical proxies computable before any LLM call include query length, clause count, named-entity density, and the presence of conjunctive sub-goals -- all of which correlate with the G1/G2 split in ToolBench. Most directly, RtP’s own top-1 cosine similarity is a zero-cost routing signal already produced by the pipeline: a high top-1 score indicates the query names an API directly (high Intent-Registry Coupling, G1-like) and can stay with RtP, whereas a low or diffuse score indicates abstract multi-step intent (G2/G3-like) that benefits from PtR’s stub decomposition -- so a simple threshold on this score routes queries with no extra model and no extra call. Stub calibration (preserving proper nouns rather than abstracting them) could further reduce G1 misrouting. For queries requiring 12+ APIs, iterative discovery (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023) may be necessary regardless of architecture.

## 5 Conclusion

We present a systematic head-to-head comparison of Retrieve-then-Plan and Plan-then-Retrieve at industrial scale (50k APIs). Three findings stand out. First, there is a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP wins on single-tool queries; PtR wins significantly on intra-category multi-tool queries (G2: recall +0.045, _p\<_0.001, _n_=200) and directionally on cross-category queries (G3: recall +0.012, _n_=100, not significant individually; pass rate difference is significant). This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (_k_=1-20), every registry size (1k-47k APIs), and replicates on gpt-oss-120b, confirming the result is architectural rather than model- specific. Second, stub hallucination is a double-edged sword: it destroys high-coupling signals on simple queries but productively decomposes multi-faceted intent on complex ones. Third, the retrieval step is the binding constraint on agent behavior: planners faithfully execute whatever tools they are given (at least 96% fidelity), so architecture choice at retrieval time largely determines the downstream trajectory. These findings motivate complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction: directing single-tool queries to RtP and multi-tool queries to PtR reduces discovery-call overhead by ∼36% with no retrieval quality loss. A cross-model replication on gpt-oss-120b (Appendix J) confirms the crossover directions are consistent across model families.

## Limitations

This work is scoped as a controlled architectural comparison: we isolate the retrieval paradigm as the single varying factor, holding the planner, embedding model, and benchmark fixed (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GTE-base, ToolBench). This design choice enables clean attribution; Appendix J provides an initial replication on gpt-oss-120b confirming the crossover directions hold across model families, though generalization to other registry types (e.g., enterprise-internal APIs with different naming conventions) remains to be validated. ## I Scaling Study Details

Sub-registries are constructed by including all Ground-Truth APIs for the subset under study plus proportionally sampled distractor APIs from all 50 ToolBench categories to reach the target size; the G1 and G2 recall curves use their respective Ground-Truth sets, and the divergence column is measured on the G1 sub- registries. Each size is run with 5 random seeds (different distractor samples); the full registry (46,984 APIs) has no randomness and is run once. Because G2’s Ground-Truth set (1,048 APIs) already exceeds the 1k target, the smallest G2 point is gold-only, slightly larger than 1k, and has zero seed variance. PtR reuses the saved stubs from the main experiment (stub generation is independent of registry size), so no additional LLM calls are made; only FAISS retrieval is recomputed per sub-registry.  10 reports the full numerical results.

The main findings replicate. On G1, RtP outperforms PtR on precision (+0.088), recall (+0.113), and pass rate (+0.069). On G2, PtR outperforms RtP on precision (+0.039) and recall (+0.051); pass rate is a statistical tie (0.826\(\pm\)0.029 vs. 0.820\(\pm\)0.029). On G3, RtP has higher precision (0.135 vs. 0.123\(\pm\)0.008, n.s.) and recall (0.160 vs. 0.146\(\pm\)0.008, _p_=0.035) while PtR leads on pass rate (0.805\(\pm\)0.013 vs. 0.790\(\pm\)0.008, n.s.); unlike Gemini, the small G3 recall gap reverses toward RtP here, underscoring that G3 (the smallest set) is the least stable across model families. RtP retrieval metrics are identical to the Gemini results, confirming they depend only on the query embedding and registry. The slightly lower PtR precision and recall for gpt- oss-120b vs. Gemini on G1 suggests stub quality varies across model families, though the crossover direction is preserved.

## K Prompts

We use two zero-shot system prompts, reproduced verbatim below. The discovery prompt (PtR only) elicits abstract tool stubs from the query alone; the planner prompt (both architectures) selects APIs from the retrieved set.

## L FAISS Index Configuration

Each API is embedded with `thenlper/gte-base` (768-dimensional, L2-normalized) from the string `"{tool\_ name}/{api\_name}: {description}"`, and all APIs are indexed with `faiss.IndexFlatIP` (exact inner- product search, equivalent to cosine similarity for normalized vectors).

Discovery prompt (stub generation)
You are a tool discovery assistant. Given a user query, identify what tools or APIs would be needed to answer it. You do NOT have access to any tool registry -instead, describe the tools you think are needed based on the query alone.

]
Be specific about tool functionality. Use snake\_case for tool names.
Planner prompt
You are a tool-augmented assistant. Given a user query and a set of available APIs, select the best API(s) to answer the query and produce a step-by-step plan.
Respond in JSON:
{
"selected\_apis": ["tool\_name/api\_name", ...],
"plan": "step-by-step plan",
"answer": "final answer to the user"
}
